content: Active management of the third stage of labor, which includes the administration of a prophylactic uterotonic, early clamping of the umbilical cord, and controlled cord traction to aid placental delivery, has been shown to reduce the risk of postpartum hemorrhage (PPH). The choice of uterotonic agent varies globally and may influence maternal outcomes. This review focuses on the use of prophylactic oxytocin during the third stage of labor to prevent PPH and other adverse maternal outcomes. Prophylactic oxytocin, when compared to no uterotonics or placebo, may reduce the risk of blood loss of 500 mL or more after delivery (risk ratio [RR] 0.51, 95% confidence interval [CI] 0.37 to 0.72; low-quality evidence) and blood loss of 1000 mL or more (RR 0.59, 95% CI 0.42 to 0.83; low-quality evidence). It likely reduces the need for additional uterotonics (RR 0.54, 95% CI 0.36 to 0.80; moderate-quality evidence). However, there may be no significant difference in the risk of requiring a blood transfusion (RR 0.88, 95% CI 0.44 to 1.78; low-quality evidence). Oxytocin may be associated with an increased risk of a prolonged third stage of labor lasting more than 30 minutes (RR 2.55, 95% CI 0.88 to 7.44; moderate-quality evidence), but the wide confidence interval suggests uncertainty about this finding. When compared to ergot alkaloids, the evidence is uncertain regarding whether oxytocin reduces the likelihood of blood loss of 500 mL or more (RR 0.84, 95% CI 0.56 to 1.25; very low-quality evidence) or the need for additional uterotonics (RR 0.89, 95% CI 0.43 to 1.81; very low-quality evidence). Similarly, the evidence is very uncertain regarding blood loss of 1000 mL or more (RR 1.13, 95% CI 0.63 to 2.01; very low-quality evidence) and the need for blood transfusion (RR 1.37, 95% CI 0.34 to 5.51; very low-quality evidence). Oxytocin probably increases the risk of a prolonged third stage of labor lasting more than 30 minutes (RR 4.69, 95% CI 1.63 to 13.45; moderate-quality evidence), but it is unclear if this leads to an increased risk of manual placental removal (RR 1.10, 95% CI 0.39 to 3.10; very low-quality evidence). Oxytocin may have little or no effect on the risk of diastolic blood pressure exceeding 100 mmHg (RR 0.28, 95% CI 0.04 to 2.05; low-quality evidence) and is probably associated with a lower risk of vomiting (RR 0.09, 95% CI 0.05 to 0.14; moderate-quality evidence). The impact of oxytocin on headaches remains uncertain (RR 0.19, 95% CI 0.03 to 1.02; very low-quality evidence). Oxytocin-ergometrine, when compared to ergot alkaloids, may slightly reduce the risk of blood loss of 500 mL or more after delivery (RR 0.44, 95% CI 0.20 to 0.94; low-quality evidence). No maternal deaths were reported in either treatment group in the one trial that assessed this outcome (moderate-quality evidence). The need for additional uterotonics was not reported in these trials. In conclusion, prophylactic oxytocin may reduce blood loss and the need for additional uterotonics when compared to no uterotonics. However, its effects compared to ergot alkaloids are uncertain, particularly regarding blood loss, the need for additional uterotonics, and blood transfusion. Oxytocin may increase the risk of a prolonged third stage of labor compared to ergot alkaloids, but it is unclear if this results in a higher likelihood of manual placental removal. The potential risks of oxytocin must be weighed against the side effects associated with ergot alkaloids. Oxytocin-ergometrine may reduce blood loss compared to ergot alkaloids, but the certainty of this evidence is low. Further high-quality trials are needed to determine the optimal dosing and administration routes for oxytocin, as well as to evaluate critical outcomes such as maternal mortality, shock, and the need for higher-level care. A planned network meta-analysis of uterotonics for PPH prevention aims to address these issues.
